title: The psychology of queues
text: Queues are a strange form of organised {{1}} (PATIENT). We join them daily, yet psychologists find them endlessly {{2}} (INTEREST). Research shows that waiting feels longer when it is {{3}} (EXPLAIN), unoccupied time is painful, and — crucially — fairness matters more than length. A queue that jumps ahead of us enrages us even when the total wait is unchanged. Airports have exploited this by moving baggage claim further from arrivals: passengers walk rather than wait, and complaints have dropped {{4}} (DRAMA). Supermarkets, meanwhile, prefer to hide the mathematics: several shorter queues feel fairer than one long queue, even when they are less {{5}} (EFFICIENT). Some companies now offer virtual queues, promising a text message instead of standing in line. The technology is {{6}} (DOUBT) clever, but it removes the chance to chat to strangers, which some sociologists regret. Queue behaviour also changes with culture: in some countries the gentle {{7}} (PRESS) of a crowd counts as a place in line, while in Britain a row of shopping baskets marks the social {{8}} (ORDER) of the queue itself.
